messages.subject: Stan Math Lib
parts:
Dear Stan members,

I am doing some self studies regarding the autodiff resources within Stan Math Lib and as an example I am trying to reproduce an adapted example of the GSL's BFGS algorithm avoiding to take analytic gradients, here the Stan shows up his power.

By the moment, everything is going very well. So, my acknowledgments about this awesome job! However, the time and RAM requirements are really massive for the following task:

In that sense, I wish to request some help to understand ways to improve the performance over a quite simple multi normal density. Up to the moment I am assuming only two parameters, mean and variance i.e., I am aware that it can be simplified to a univariate normal. But, as I said the aim is to go ahead further in structured variances and covariances.

My points are: (i) Stan Math Lib supports Eigen::Sparse? (ii) in the attached example, there is any way to avoid have an N by N matrix with stan::math::var which may compromise the efficiency of taking autodiffs? (iii) Do I am skipping any important aspect that is leveraging my time and memory needs?

BTW, I am not too confortable with the difference in time processing when I call the same function through embedded R codes (Rcpp attributes) and by means of the shared library ("sourceCpp()"). See the shared code.

P.S.: I have already tested other simplest example with sucess e.g., minimizing paraboloids.

Many thanks indeed regarding your attention over that.

Kind Regards,
FH

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Stan Math Lib
parts:
Oh, I saw the attachments at the end. Maybe that's what the
following task was after the colon?

I have no idea what any of that GSL or Rcpp stuff does.
If you can, use our built-in matrix functions which have
matrix derivatives built in so they use much less RAM. But
we don't have any sparse implementations yet. Maybe in
a year or two.

You don't ever want to create a large covariance matrix with
only a diagonal---just break it out into univariate normals.
Multivariate normals require solving the matrix, so they're
going to be O(N^3) in both memory and time for N x N matrices.

- Bob

That's a linear algebra challenge.

Not directly in that we don't have any analytic or efficient
gradients built in. But you should be able to use Stan's autodiff
types in sparse. It's usually not a win unless you have very sparse
matrices.
> (ii) in the attached example, there is any way to avoid have an N by N matrix with stan::math::var which may compromise the efficiency of taking autodiffs?

One thing you can do is reuse the 0 elements so the stack doesn't grow
as much. Or try to break it down into simpler blocks if the covariance
is block-diagonal.

messages.author: 1641d619313d04ab
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Stan Math Lib
parts:
Hi Bob,

Many many thanks regarding your reply.

I got your points. I have reworked the log of the multivariate normal to deal with this "univariate" case.

So now, instead of using the built in multi_normal_log I am doing it by myself using the Stan's matrix functions...

Thus, before I was using:
deviance = -stan::math::multi_normal_log(y, stan::math::multiply(mean, mu), stan::math::multiply(variance, Sigma));
And now, for this simple case... :

deviance = (N/2) * log(2*stan::math::pi()) + N * log(sqrt(variance)) + 0.5 * dot_self(multiply(subtract(y, mean), inv(sqrt(variance))));

Everything seems much more fast and efficient...

Thanks again...

Cheers,
FH
